"The troubled history of misjudging sentience in humans and animals

We have a very bad track record in dealing with cases of uncertain sentience.

That, for example, there was often surgery performed on newborn babies without any anaesthesia until the 1980s, because surgeons doubted that they could feel pain.

With people with brain injuries who were unresponsive,
there was this long tradition of calling them ‘vegetative’
and assuming they felt nothing, not giving them any pain relief until it became clear that sometimes they do feel what's happening to them.

And of course, there's the case of other animals as well.

If you think of chickens and fishes, shrimps–
even today people will often treat these animals as if they felt absolutely nothing.

So we've got to be aware of this risk that when we deny sentience and in fact we're wrong, there is sentience there.

We can do really appalling things.

We can end up treating those systems really, really badly.

We should be mindful about that risk when thinking about the case of AI."
